name: Jawline hammer tools

lead: Jawline hammer tools, also called face hammers, are hammers or similar implements marketed or discussed for striking the face and jaw, with the aim of a more defined jawline and cheekbones. They are associated with bonesmashing, the idea that hitting facial bones can remodel them.

Proponents say repeated impact stimulates bone to remodel. No published study has tested these tools, and the sources available describe the practice mainly through media coverage and surgeon commentary. Surgeons writing in journals describe the trend as dangerous.

paras: People describe using the tool to strike the jaw or cheekbones repeatedly over time, as part of the wider bonehacks category of looksmaxxing.
Facial surgeons cite fractures, misalignment, neurovascular injury, deformity and vision changes as possible outcomes.

lead: Jawline hammer tools, also called face hammers, are hammers or similar implements marketed or discussed for striking the face and jaw in the belief that doing so reshapes bone. They are associated with bonesmashing, a looksmaxxing practice in which people hit their facial bones in the hope of remodeling them [1].
No published study has tested such tools, and the sources available describe the underlying practice mainly through media coverage and surgeon commentary [1].

paras: Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes bonesmashing as hitting one's face with an object such as a hammer to achieve a chiselled look, and says the practice is rarely carried out and is regarded by some as an inside joke; sources it cites describe it as misinformation [1]. The article does not describe specific commercial products.

Facial surgeons quoted in coverage cited by Wikipedia warn that striking the face risks fractures, misalignment, neurovascular injury, deformity and changes to vision [1]. Letters in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery have also raised concern about bone smashing as a social-media trend. See the bonesmashing article for fuller coverage.
